transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, um, I guess I'm here because things at work have just gotten completely out of hand. I work in transit, I'm a driver, and I know how the system works, I've been doing this for a while. You have your logs, your GPS, the standard stuff, which is fine. I don't mind the standard stuff. But recently, dispatch and the compliance department—especially compliance—they’ve been tracking my route changes in a way that is definitely not standard. 

They’re using the computer system to flag every single tiny deviation I make. Like, if I take a slightly different street to avoid a backup, suddenly there are these... these little comments coming through on the two-way radio. Just little remarks, sometimes just a tone of voice or a specific word, that might seem like nothing to anyone else, but I know exactly what they mean. They're letting me know they see me. 

And, you know, when I try to bring it up, when I tell people what's happening, they just brush me off and say it’s just normal oversight. They say, 'Oh, everyone gets monitored, it's just protocol, it's for efficiency.' But it's not just protocol. It really isn't. Because I can tell that certain drivers are reporting on me, too. I see them at the depot, I see how they look at me when I'm doing my pre-trip inspection, and then suddenly dispatch knows things about my route that they couldn't just get from the computer screen. The other drivers are feeding information back to compliance, and it's just... it's exhausting trying to do my job when you know everyone is coordinating to watch your every single move like that.
Do you feel that people are watching or following you outside of work, or that this kind of monitoring is happening in other areas of your life?

Well, um, outside of work? I mean, that's a really good question, because you'd think it would just be at the depot, right? You'd think it's just a work thing, just compliance being compliance. But, honestly, I haven't really seen that same level of... of coordination outside of my shifts. 

Like, when I go to the grocery store or when I'm just running errands around my neighborhood, I don't get that same feeling that people are reporting on me. I mean, sure, sometimes people look at you a little too long in the checkout line, but that's just normal city living, you know? It's not like the other drivers. It's not like dispatch. At work, it's this whole system, this whole network of them communicating about me. But when I'm off the clock, when I'm just in my own car or walking down my street, I don't have that same sense of being tracked. I don't see the same cars following me, I don't hear those little coded remarks from people passing by. 

It's really just focused on my job, which almost makes it worse in a way, because it means they are specifically targeting my livelihood, my career. They want to find something wrong with my driving, my routes. So, no, I wouldn't say it's happening everywhere. It's very specific to work. Very specific.

Have you ever felt that thoughts are being placed in your mind that aren't your own, or that events or actions around you are specifically directed at you in a personal way that others don't seem to notice?

Thoughts placed in my mind? Like, someone else putting them there? No, um, no, absolutely not. I know my own mind. I really do. You know, when you drive a large transit vehicle for a living, you have to be completely sharp, constantly aware of your surroundings, the pedestrians, the traffic lights, the blind spots—you have to have a very clear head to manage all that safely. So my thoughts are entirely my own. I don't feel like someone is beaming things into my brain or anything bizarre like you see in those late-night sci-fi movies. I'm just a regular person trying to do my job. Every thought I have about the routes, about the compliance department, or even just what I'm going to make for dinner when I get home—that's all me. Nobody is putting anything in there. I'm a very analytical person, I have my associate's degree, I think things through very carefully, so I would definitely notice if a thought wasn't mine. 

And as for events or actions being directed at me... well, I mean, aside from what I was just telling you about work, no. Like I said, the dispatchers, the other drivers, the compliance people—that's real, that's actually happening on the radio and at the depot. They are directing those little comments at me. But it's not like... I don't know, it's not like the television is speaking to me, or the streetlights are blinking just for me when I drive past them, or billboards have secret messages. I've read about things like that, where people think the news anchors are talking directly to them through the screen, but I don't have anything like that going on at all. It's just my workplace. I just have a very real, very specific issue with my employer overstepping their bounds and coordinating against me. But my mind? My mind is completely my own, one hundred percent. I don't have any confusion about what's inside my own head.
Have you ever had beliefs or ideas that other people have trouble understanding or don’t seem to agree with, even when you’ve tried to explain them clearly?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, that's exactly what I've been talking about with the whole situation at work, right? It's incredibly frustrating because I try to explain it to people, and I try to be very clear and logical about it. I lay out the facts. I tell them, look, dispatch and compliance are tracking my route changes through the computer system. And I explain how it's not just the GPS—it's the little comments on the radio, the specific wording they use to let me know they're watching. 

But when I tell people this, when I try to get them to understand the sheer scale of what's happening, they just... they don't get it. Or they don't want to get it. They just give me this look and say, "Oh, it's just normal oversight, everybody gets monitored, it's for efficiency." And I have to explain to them again, no, you aren't listening to me. It's not normal oversight. Normal oversight is checking the logs at the end of the week. Normal oversight isn't having certain drivers reporting on me at the depot. I can tell they are doing it, I see the way they look at me during the pre-trip inspections, and then suddenly compliance knows things they shouldn't know. 

I've tried explaining this to my sister, I've tried explaining it to a couple of friends outside of work, and they just have so much trouble understanding it. They think I'm just stressed or overreacting to standard protocol. But it's like, how can you not see it? How can you not see that it's a coordinated effort? It's so obvious to me, the way the drivers feed information back to compliance, the way the radio comments line up perfectly with my route deviations... but no matter how clearly I break it down, no matter how many examples I give them, they just don't seem to agree. They just brush it off. And it's exhausting, it really is, trying to make people see something that is happening right in front of them when they just refuse to understand the reality of the situation.

Can you tell me if the people you believe are involved in this monitoring—like dispatch, compliance, and other drivers—are all acting together with a shared purpose, or if they each have their own separate reasons for what they’re doing?

Oh, they are absolutely acting together. It is a completely unified effort, one hundred percent. Because, if you think about how a transit depot operates, it is a strict hierarchy. You have the drivers out on the ground, you have dispatch running the immediate logistics over the airwaves, and then you have compliance sitting in the back office looking at all the data. They could not pull this off if they were not all on the exact same page. 

I mean, the whole reason I am here talking to you about this is because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system, and they coordinate it with those little comments on the radio. It is a continuous, closed loop of information. Dispatch sees something on the screen, they make a specific comment on the radio, and then the other drivers hear it and know exactly what to look for. And even when people say it is just normal oversight, like when people try to tell me they track everyone for standard metrics and efficiency, I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me. I see them in the breakroom. I see the way they shift their posture or look down at their clipboards when I walk in, and then suddenly compliance knows exactly what happened at a specific intersection on my morning run. 

If they were just doing their own separate things, it would be completely chaotic. Like, one driver might just have a personal grudge, or one dispatcher might just be a micromanager having a bad day. But this is seamless. The computer system flags my route, the radio comments confirm it, and the drivers act as the eyes on the ground for the compliance officers. They all share the exact same purpose, which is to build this massive, coordinated file on my performance to use against me. It takes a massive amount of effort and communication to run a network like that behind the scenes, making sure every piece of data lines up perfectly. So yes, it is highly coordinated. They are all working together, hand in glove, and it just proves how much time and energy they are dedicating specifically to me.

Even though others have told you that what you're experiencing is standard oversight and there's no coordinated effort against you, do you still believe with complete certainty that dispatch, compliance, and certain drivers are working together specifically to target and undermine you at work?

Yes. Yes, without a shadow of a doubt. I mean, I know what other people say, I hear them when they try to dismiss it, but they aren't the ones sitting behind the wheel of a transit vehicle for eight, nine, sometimes ten hours a day. They don't see how the pieces fit together. 

Honestly, the whole reason I’m even here in this office talking to you right now is because dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes through the computer system, and they've been doing it relentlessly. It's not just a casual glance at a screen. It's the computer system logging my exact coordinates, and then it's the little comments on the radio that immediately follow, confirming that they're watching my exact movements. Like, if I have to brake a little harder than usual because a pedestrian stepped off the curb, within thirty seconds there's a radio check using a specific phrase about "maintaining proper pacing." 

And it's incredibly frustrating because even when people say it’s just normal oversight—that everyone's GPS gets monitored for efficiency, or that it's just standard company policy to check the logs—I know it's not. I know the difference between a routine audit and being actively targeted. I have my associate's degree, I understand how data collection works, and this goes way beyond that. Because I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me, too. I can literally see it happening. Just the other day, I had to take a slight detour around a stalled delivery truck on 4th Street, and the moment I got back to the depot, another driver—one who didn't even have a route near mine—was walking out of the compliance office, looking right at me and tapping his radio. You don't do that for normal oversight. You just don't. 

So yes, I am absolutely, one hundred percent certain they are all working together to undermine me. It’s a massive, coordinated effort, and it’s happening every single shift. It doesn't matter how many times someone tries to tell me it's just standard procedure, because they aren't the ones living it. I am. And I see exactly what they are doing.

latest_inference.note: The patient's belief that dispatch, compliance, and other drivers are engaged in a coordinated, deliberate effort to target and undermine them—despite others attributing it to standard oversight—represents a delusional system that is non-bizarre and persistent, consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22.0). The other candidates (mood disorders with psychotic features and PTSD) are ruled out due to absence of mood episodes, hallucinations, or trauma-related symptoms.
